title: 12 year game dev, and this is my first AI game
author: Certain_Ad9908
selftext:
Code & Art are 100% made with AI  
My role: game design, code architecture, art direction & QA

Built solo for the DreamLayer AI game jam in 8 days. You can try it at: [https://motawe3.itch.io/underbloom](https://motawe3.itch.io/underbloom)

Built with: Unity 6, Claude Opus 5.5, DreamLayerAI, and Magnific.  
More details on how it was built are on the game page.

replies.author: Aridjen
replies.body:
Steam, for example, needs to verify games more thoroughly instead of just releasing everything for profit.

 And the developers themselves need to do everything more carefully. For instance, I’m currently working on a game with AI — I’ve already been at it for a month; I have two accounts, each worth $200, and the development will definitely take another month. I’ve already spent around $20,000.

replies.author: Laicbeias
replies.body:
I think they cant. We need something that lets you audit yourself and track how something was build and how much human input and iteration there was. If we dont game dev wont make it.

And 2 months.. i dont want to say thats bad. But thats the problem. If you work iterative that shouldnt get you far. If you work generative you let llms do decisions and choose for you. Even with good planning, if you care half the work is deciding what to get rid of, after you see it and judging if it is a good experience. You cant do that with llms, it requires taste.

Thats the part that llms dont automate. And worse. Since you now can generate content en mass, those who work like that will have it harder. Because this kind of work is invisible and the center of any good game ever made. So yeah we are about to murder gaming

replies.author: Aridjen
replies.body:
That’s exactly it — it’s all about the taste, and you won’t be able to make a good game quickly with AI, especially when it’s a multiplayer game.

Here’s a frame from my game — is there any taste here?

replies.author: Disastrous_Toe_7169
replies.body: Do you feel this is better overall for the gamer? I think it will make it easier for enthusiasts to showcase ideas. Being part of the industry do you feel this is bad for the industry quality wise?

replies.author: Certain_Ad9908
replies.body: Imagine a day when anyone can build a car. It will open doors for people with brilliant automotive concepts, but we'll also spend far more time sorting through a sea of amateur prototypes to find them.

replies.author: Disastrous_Toe_7169
replies.body: Kind of I believe. I feel like gaming has had to compromise passion for profit and the accessibility of tools such as RPG maker and godot has made gems more common. Also I believe that if you embark on the journey of building a car you love cars enough to go through the hassle so quality should improve. I don’t know maybe I’m being naive. I see it from my industry as a SaaS. Everyone says SaaS are dying but I can’t see anyone building what I built not because of lack of tools but lack of specialized knowledge. More people expressing themselves through their passions is good.

replies.author: Certain_Ad9908
replies.body: I get your point. Maybe domain knowledge gives you an edge in SaaS. For indie game devs, one of the toughest challenges we've faced was getting our games seen. With AI and large-scale enablement, the noise has increased. This issue doesn't really affect big studios with huge marketing budgets. Eventually, these tools won't go away, but we'll adapt.

replies.author: Disastrous_Toe_7169
replies.body: Thanks for your insights! Wishing you luck and notoriety on your projects!

replies.author: Certain_Ad9908
replies.body: Thanks a lot! Best of luck with your SaaS endeavors as well.

replies.author: Certain_Ad9908
replies.body: Thanks! For code, I've set up a stage-by-stage process with Claude for the whole game after creating the design document and art references. Claude code (Opus 5.5, high effort) then started each stage as an orchestration session, running other sub-agents as needed. For art, Claude drove DreamLayer AI and Magnific MCPs for generation, and used more Magnific for cleanup (background removal and splitting creature rigs). Other assets/tools used: I've set up Master Audio 2024 for audio mixing and Feel for VFX, both were used pretty well by Claude. From there, I took on QA as each stage finished, and I prevented starting other stages until the current one was accepted. All the way to publishing.

comments.author: fukinrage85
comments.body: How did you paint the ground textures?

replies.author: Certain_Ad9908
replies.body: Not painted.  The game has multiple regions, each with one texture from GPT Image via Magnific. Prompt tip: "tileable" made it draw paving tiles, more on the prompt I asked for a "uniform material swatch, no focal point" instead. Claude then created a Unity editor tool that blends each texture with a half-offset copy of itself to make it seamless. Lastly, a custom URP 2D shader does the rest. It samples each texture at two scales mixed by noise so the tiling doesn't show, blends the regions with a splat map, and adds worn paths plus soft shadows around rocks. Decals and ground cover that bends when creatures walk through it go on top.

replies.author: fukinrage85
replies.body: Got it. Understood. I had tried stochastic blending and trilinear blending but never got that really natural look. I'll incorporate your process. I appreciate it.

comments.author: EuphoricIncrease3645
comments.body:
Don’t say is an ai game. I’m getting tired of that.

What does actually mean (in general)? How much is AI?

What is important to me:  
Did you designed it?  
Did you iterate until it was fun?  
Did you iterate until it reached your visual vision?  
Does it have it have challenges that you feel push the player skills?  
How much play time does it have?

replies.author: Certain_Ad9908
replies.body:
I understand what you mean. In general, what I mean is I didn't write a single line of code or craft a piece of art manually, yet I built something in about a week that would have taken a team and me a few months. So yes, AI carried the development, and I directed it.

That's fundamentally different from AI quickies that are designed, tested, and validated by AI.

Designed it? Yes. The concept, the grafting mechanic, and the creature design are mine, and I reviewed and approved the design doc. (This was the most important part really)

Iterated until fun? Definitely. I playtested every stage and sent it back until it felt right.

Iterated to my visual vision? Yes. I approved every piece of art, and I rerolled many.

Challenge? Yes. Mechanics and balancing were on and off until it felt right. This is not even finished yet.

Play time? A run is about 6–10 minutes (20-30 if you want to explore)

replies.author: EuphoricIncrease3645
replies.body:
Thanks for the reply. It sounds great!  
It means this is not an AI game.

I challenge you to continue iterating. Don’t stop here!

But now i’m finally able to make a ‘game’ I have been dreaming of for the last years… i’m simply not able to code at home, be a good partner and father… but with AI i’m now making my dream ‘game’ (not really a game in the sense of gaming but won’t go into this too much for now) and it’s starting look fleshed out! Ideas get thrown around by me and my spouse/kids and I can just let it try it for us, and if it doesn’t work do a rollback on git etc etc… is the code perfect? Is the code human readable? Not sure didn’t even look yet but right now the game runs amazing and does what I want it to do!

Also going to work on some kid games to teach them typing (not many in Dutch that I find fit) and do simple math etc
